storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of thunderstorms is tracking in from about 46 miles to the west and could reach the cove around 6 PM, but the cool Long Island Sound should weaken or slow it down more than what inland neighbors will see.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer strong now (10°F air–water gap) and still holding around 10°F when the nearest cell is projected to cross near 6 PM, but the gap fades below the 5°F choke threshold by 7:57 PM as the evening cools.
storm.detail_html:
OKX radar shows a cluster of cells (max 38 dBZ) about 46 miles west of the cove, tracking east-southeast at roughly 24 kt. The latest area forecast discussion flags a Severe Thunderstorm Watch through 9 PM, but mainly for areas well to our west — the NYC metro and Nassau County on Long Island. No watch or warning is currently posted for Riverside/Greenwich itself, and forecasters note real uncertainty in how far east the stronger storms ultimately get.

The Sound is running 73.9°F against air near 84°F, a 10.3°F gap that supports a moderate marine stable layer — the cushion of cooler, denser air that tends to choke off low-level convection as storms cross the water. That gap holds essentially flat through the early evening, and the nearest cell is projected to still be crossing into roughly a 9.7°F gap when it arrives — enough to earn the protective discount. But the buffer isn't permanent: the gap drops below the ~5°F threshold where the effect stops working around 7:57 PM, about 20 minutes before sunset, as the air cools faster than the Sound. Anything arriving after that gets no protective credit.

The nearest cell's ETA is 6:03 PM, with a window of 5:38–6:47 PM (medium confidence, based on a 25-minute radar-centroid motion measurement). CAPE is modest right now (800 J/kg) but climbs through the evening in the extended outlook (roughly 1,100–1,800 J/kg), with strong shear (34 kt) favoring organized storms. The low current CAPE keeps punch-through risk low for this first wave.

What would change the call: if the watch verifies eastward and cells reorganize closer or stronger — inside 25 miles at 45+ dBZ — or NWS issues a warning covering this area, upgrade to high. Any later-developing cell arriving after roughly 8 PM should be treated as arriving at full strength, since the marine layer buffer will already be gone by then.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 46 mi W closing at 24 kt; the marine layer is still standing at arrival (~10°F gap) and may weaken it or push arrival late.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze holds the S-SSW axis through the first half of the window, then backs to a lighter WSW gradient breeze after the 7:29 PM thermal collapse; start mid-line and expect the pressure to even out across the course as the evening goes on.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a sea-breeze day reinforced by a light onshore gradient (sea breeze reinforced by the background wind, internal code A+): the air-water temperature gap (deltaT) is 10.3°F, well above the 5°F threshold that gets a thermal circulation going, and the background synoptic flow is a light southwest wind around 6 kt — onshore and under 15 kt, so it reinforces rather than fights the sea breeze. Station ensemble confidence is moderate: 48% of coastal stations are already reading southerly, with the over-water buoy fully onshore.

HRRR's own forecast direction lags reality by a wide margin right now — it's calling for E at 95° while western-LIS stations are already reading S at 179°, an 84° divergence. The fetcher's maturation correction only closes part of that gap (to ESE 110° for the near-term forecast), so this briefing leans on observed direction for the current hour and the cove skill's typical mature-SB progression (S through SSW) for the next couple of hours, rather than trusting the raw model number. Direction confidence is rated moderate — worth a grain of salt on exact degrees, less so on the general S-to-SSW-then-WSW arc.

With S-SSW flow early in the window, the geography table calls this the cleanest, most uniform flow the cove sees — steadiest pressure, little to choose between the two shores. As the breeze backs toward WSW after the 7:29 PM collapse (about 30 minutes ahead of the 7:59 PM sunset), expect it to channel down the Sound axis: still steady in direction, but with more pressure mid-Sound than tight against the CT shore, and puffier/patchier than the S phase.

Shift character: through 6 PM this is a mature, oscillating sea breeze — play the shifts, don't overcommit. Through 7 PM it becomes a persistent backing shift as the thermal winds down and the gradient reasserts — commit to the new direction rather than expecting it to swing back. After the collapse it settles into steady gradient flow with normal gust/lull cycling, no further persistent shift expected.

Speed-wise this reads as a one-design sweet spot through the first half of the window (6-8 kt, gusting to 12), easing into light-air/drifter range (5-6 kt) once the thermal drops out around 8 PM. Not a big-breeze evening, but raceable throughout — expect the back half of a series to feel noticeably lighter than the front half.
